title: What belongs on your website, social media and in a video?
description: A practical guide for small business owners deciding what should live on the website, what belongs on social media, and when video or campaign content is worth making.
summary: Your website should hold the durable source of truth: core services, proof, location, pricing context and the action you want people to take. Social media is for discovery, repeated exposure and current conversation. Video is best for explaining, showing craft and helping people feel what your business does. Campaign content should send people back to a focused website action.
takeaways: Let the website carry the stable buying information, not the daily content treadmill.
Use social media for discovery and repeated contact, then send serious interest back to a focused page.
Invest in video when explanation, emotion, demonstrations or trust signals change the buying decision.

sections.title: Start with the website, not the feed
sections.body:
The website should be the place where the business is easiest to understand. It needs the core offer, the service areas, the proof, the buying path and enough context for a visitor to know whether you are a good fit. Social media can bring in attention, and video can explain the story, but neither should force a customer to guess what you actually do.

That matters because small businesses rarely have time to keep every channel equally fresh. A useful website keeps working between campaigns. It can answer the same important questions for months or years, while your social posts and videos bring people toward those answers at the right moment.

sections.title: The website holds the durable source of truth
sections.body:
Put the stable information on the website: what you do, who it is for, where you work, how to start, what makes the offer different and what evidence supports it. A strong website design and development project also makes room for useful next steps, such as an enquiry form, booking path, sample or call to action.

This is especially important for service businesses. A landscaping company, accommodation, school, parish or repair service does not need every social post to explain the whole business. The website can carry the main structure, while other channels create reasons to visit it.

sections.title: Social media is for discovery and repeated contact
sections.body:
Social media is good at starting or restarting attention. People may not be searching for your service today, but a useful post, a short clip, a customer story or a clear graphic can make your business easier to remember later. The job is not to hold every important fact. The job is to create recognition and give people a reason to take another look.

That is why social assets should connect to your wider brand deliverables. The words, images, colours and tone should feel related to the website. A visitor should not arrive on your site and wonder whether they found the same business.

sections.title: Video explains, demonstrates and moves people
sections.body:
Video is worth making when the message benefits from motion, voice, demonstration or human presence. A founder can explain a misunderstood service more clearly than a paragraph can. A film can show the feeling of a place, the care behind a process or the difference a community project makes. That was the useful job in work such as the AI Catalyst video, the Vertical Impression product story and the St. James School donor film: the medium helped people understand something that was easy to overlook.

Video also needs practical planning. Captions, transcripts, clear audio and readable on-screen text help more people use the work, and the W3C's accessible media guidance is a useful reference before production. Good craft matters here because viewers make quick judgments about clarity, care and credibility.

sections.title: A campaign link should close the loop
sections.body:
The campaign link is where scattered attention becomes a useful action. A social post can introduce the idea, and a video can make the idea easier to care about, but the linked page should tell the visitor exactly what to do next. That might be booking a consultation, requesting a quote, watching a longer film, reading a service page or donating through an approved process.

Do not send every campaign to the homepage if the homepage cannot answer the campaign's question. A focused page can repeat the promise in the visitor's language, provide the right proof and reduce the number of choices. That is often more useful than asking a cold visitor to wander through the whole website.

sections.title: A sample week of website, social and video content
sections.body:
Suppose a small Okanagan service business wants better enquiries for one core offer. The week does not need to become a full-time publishing operation. It needs one clear source of truth, a few useful social assets and one piece of richer content where it will help.

Sample small business content split
ChannelWhat it holdsExample for one week
WebsiteService details, proof, service area, process and enquiry pathImprove one core service page and add a focused campaign section
Social mediaDiscovery, reminders, short stories, campaign posts and conversationThree posts: one problem, one proof point, one invitation to enquire
VideoExplanation, demonstration, founder presence or emotional storyOne short clip answering the question customers ask before booking
Campaign linkThe next stepSend all campaign traffic to the improved service page or a focused landing page

This kind of plan keeps the website from becoming a stream of temporary posts, while also keeping social from becoming a place where important buying information disappears.

sections.title: Choose the mix that fits the way people buy
sections.body:
Not every business needs the same amount of video. A highly visual service may benefit from short demonstrations, while a complex service may need a clearer founder-led explanation. A local business with repeat demand may get more from consistent social reminders and strong reviews than from a large film. The tradeoff is time, production cost and the ability to keep the work current.

Ask what the buyer still does not understand before they enquire. If the answer is a process, show the process. If the answer is trust, show the people and the care behind the work. If the answer is fit, make the website page clearer first. A practical marketing and branding project should connect those pieces rather than treat each channel as a separate contest.

sections.title: Make one page easier to act on
sections.body:
A useful next step is to choose one important service and write down four things: the website promise, the proof, the social angle and the question a short video could answer. If those four notes do not line up, the content plan will feel scattered before production starts. If they do line up, each asset has a clear job.

You do not need to publish everywhere at once. You need a durable website message, a few social assets that create recognition and richer media where it helps people choose. If you want to talk through that mix for your business, book a free consultation and we can look at what should come first.

faqs: Should every social media post also become a website page?

No. Most social posts are reminders, conversation starters or campaign moments. Turn a social idea into website content when it answers a durable buying question, explains a service clearly or deserves search visibility over time.
What accessibility basics should a small business video include?

Start with clear speech, low background noise, captions and a transcript. Add visual description or careful scripting when important information appears only on screen, and choose a player that lets people control playback.
How much video should a small business make before hiring help?

Make enough to test the message honestly: a simple explanation, a short customer-facing answer or a basic demonstration can show whether the topic holds attention. Bring in help when story, filming, editing or accessibility requirements are beyond your available time.
How should social posts and video send people to the website?

Give each piece a specific destination matching what the viewer has just seen: a service, project, campaign or booking page. Keep the message and next step consistent across that handoff. A generic homepage link can work for broad awareness, but a detailed service story should lead to equally relevant information.
What should stay on the website instead of living only on social media?

Keep current service details, location, important practical questions and the contact route on pages the business controls. Use social media for updates, discovery and conversation. When a post answers an enduring customer question, turn the useful information into website content so future visitors do not have to search through old posts.
